MAIB AI 221 · COMPUTER VISION · FINAL PROJECT 4 · RETAIL

ShelfWatch

Finding empty shelf space from one phone photo, and turning it into a restock list.

Prerna Gade
Live app: https://shelfwatch.streamlit.app/
GitHub: https://github.com/Prerna-02/shelfwatch

Speaker notes: Hello everyone. My project is ShelfWatch, for the retail sector. A store associate takes one photo of a shelf, and the app finds every empty spot and tells them what to restock first. Everything you will see is free and open: the model runs on a CPU, and the app is live at shelfwatch.streamlit.app.

THE PROBLEM

An empty spot on a shelf is a sale that walks out of the store

Who

Store associate or area manager

Photographs a shelf with a phone during a walk-round.

Decision it supports

What to restock first

Shelves are checked irregularly; gaps go unnoticed for hours.

What an error costs

Two mistakes, two costs

Missed gap: a lost sale. False gap: a wasted trip to the shelf.

Speaker notes: The problem: when a shelf spot is empty, a customer who wanted that item walks away. Staff only check shelves now and then. The user is a store associate with a phone; the decision is what to restock first. And there are two kinds of error: a missed gap costs a sale, a false gap wastes a trip. I will come back to these two errors in every result.

Speaker notes: This is the architecture. Two halves, joined by one file. The top half runs once on a free Colab GPU: I take a subset of SKU-110K, fine-tune YOLO11n, export it to a 10 megabyte ONNX file, and evaluate it on the test set and on my own store photos; the LaMa experiment also runs here. That model file is copied into the app. The bottom half runs for every photo on a CPU in about half a second: check the photo and blur people, find products with the model, group them into shelf rows, find gaps and check that each one really looks empty, and show the restock list. Only the highlighted step uses the trained model; everything after it is classical computer vision on the boxes.

DATA

Crowded shelves to learn from, real stores to test on

SKU-110K (CVPR 2019, research use)

11,743

shelf photos, a box on every product. We trained on a 30% subset: 2,466 photos.

How crowded

138

products in a typical photo, up to 718; each about 5% of the photo’s width.

Our real-world test set

40

photos from local stores, with permission; 108 gaps drawn by hand before seeing the app’s output.

SKU-110K shelves are almost always full, so real gaps are rare in it. That is why we also test on our own photos, and why the generative step tries to make synthetic gaps.

Speaker notes: Data. For training I used SKU-110K, a public research dataset of over eleven thousand shelf photos with a box on every product. It is very crowded: about 138 products per photo and up to 718, which is why I raised YOLO's default limit of 300 boxes to 1,000 and trained at 960 pixels. For a real-world test I photographed 40 shelves in local stores and drew 108 gaps by hand, following a written rule, before looking at the app's results.

BEFORE VS AFTER FINE-TUNING

From 0 products found to 126 of 126

Box quality, mAP@0.5 (test set)

0.30 → 0.92

Products found, recall at 0.35

2% → 86%

Product count error per photo

97% → 10%

COCO-trained YOLO11n, output swapped for one class, 50 epochs on 2,466 shelf photos (3 h, free Colab GPU).

Before: COCO model, 0 boxes

After: fine-tuned, 126 of 126

Speaker notes: Before and after. The off-the-shelf YOLO11n, trained on COCO, has never seen the class "shelf product": on this shelf with 126 products it drew zero boxes. Fine-tuning means starting from those COCO weights, swapping the 80-class output for one class, and training on shelf photos. After 3 hours on a free GPU it finds all 126. On the whole test set: mAP at 0.5 went from 0.30 to 0.92, it finds 86% of products instead of 2%, and the count error fell from 97% to 10%. Validation loss fell with training loss, so it did not overfit.

EVALUATION ON HELD-OUT DATA

Strong on the test set, weaker on the most crowded shelves

TestResult
SKU-110K test set, 2,935 photosmAP@0.5 0.92 · precision 0.90 · recall 0.85
Shelf density: sparse / medium / denseRecall 0.87 / 0.90 / 0.82
App model (ONNX) vs PyTorchmAP 0.917 vs 0.915: nothing lost
Confidence threshold0.35, best F1 on validation photos

Densest shelves have the smallest products, so more are missed, and a missed product looks like a gap.

Speaker notes: Evaluation on held-out data. On all 2,935 test photos the model scores 0.92 mAP, with 90% precision and 85% recall. Splitting the shelves by how crowded they are, recall drops to 0.82 on the densest third. I exported the model to ONNX so it runs on a free CPU server, and checked that this loses nothing. The confidence threshold of 0.35 was chosen on validation photos, not on the test set. It runs in about half a second per photo.

REAL STORES: 40 PHOTOS, 108 HAND-DRAWN GAPS

An emptiness check made the restock list twice as trustworthy

Gaps vs hand labelsRecallPrecisionF1
Gap finder alone0.810.300.44
With emptiness check, red list0.670.540.60
Red + orange (check by eye)0.81——

Empty shelf = few edges; a missed product still has print. Tuned on 20 photos, tested on the other 20: precision 0.29 → 0.55. Busy gaps stay visible in orange.

Speaker notes: The real-world test. On my 40 store photos, the gap finder alone found 81% of the gaps I drew, but only 30% of what it flagged was real: too many false alarms, mostly products it missed. So I added an emptiness check using edge detection from Lecture 2. I chose its cut-off on the odd-numbered photos and tested on the even ones: precision almost doubled. It costs some recall, so instead of deleting busy gaps the app shows them in orange for a human to check.

GENERATIVE AI: SYNTHETIC EMPTY SHELVES

LaMa painted the products back

Original: two products to erase

Classical fill: empty · 56% found

LaMa fill: ghost products · 5% found

On 100 test shelves the detector saw a product in 83% of LaMa holes (classical: 3%). LaMa continues the surrounding pattern, and on a shelf that pattern is products. A measured negative result: it needs guidance, such as text-guided inpainting with “empty shelf”.

Speaker notes: The generative AI part. Real gaps are rare in the training data, so the plan was to make our own: erase a few products and let LaMa, an open inpainting model, fill the hole with empty shelf. We know exactly where each fake gap is, so we can test the gap finder. Here is one example. In the middle, the classical fill just smears nearby pixels: it looks fake, but empty, and the gap finder found 56% of these holes. On the right, LaMa: it continues the pattern, and on a shelf the pattern is products, so it repainted faded ghost products. The detector saw a product in 83% of its holes and found only 5% of the gaps. This is a measured, explained negative result. The fix is a generative model you can tell what to paint, like text-guided inpainting with the prompt "empty shelf".

RESULTS BY SHELF TYPE · OUR 40 STORE PHOTOS

Works on open shelves and fridges, fails on flat chocolate bars

Open shelves · 27 photos, 93 gaps

0.65

Gap F1 · recall 0.68, precision 0.62

Glass-door fridges · 5 photos, 12 gaps

0.61

Gap F1 · recall 0.67, precision 0.56

Chocolate, flat bars · 8 photos, 3 gaps

0.09

Gap F1 · flat bars are missed, so their space looks empty

Groups of 5 and 8 photos give rough numbers only. The model learned from SKU-110K stores, mostly outside our region: flat, lying products and glass doors are rare there.

Speaker notes: Results by shelf type, which is my bias check. On open shelves the app works reasonably: F1 0.65. Glass fridges are similar. But on chocolate displays it fails: flat bars lying down look nothing like the upright bottles and boxes in the training data, so the model misses them, and every missed bar looks like an empty space. The fridge and chocolate groups are small, so treat those numbers as rough. The lesson is domain shift: a model trained on other countries' stores needs local data.

RESPONSIBLE AI

Help staff restock, never watch people

Privacy

People are pixelated before the photo is shown. No photo is stored. Our store photos stay out of the public repo.

Human in the loop

Red = restock, orange = check by eye. “Not sure” warnings for blurry photos, people in front, low confidence.

Fair use

Not for monitoring or judging staff. Research-only training data: not for commercial use.

Drift and bias

Weaker on local formats (flat bars, fridges). Re-test in each new store type. Documented in the model card.

Speaker notes: Responsible AI. Privacy: people are detected and pixelated, and nothing is stored. Human in the loop: the app never acts on its own; red and orange and the "not sure" warnings tell staff how much to trust each result. Fair use: it must not become a staff-monitoring tool, and the training data is research-only. And drift: we saw it is weaker on local formats, so it should be re-tested in each new store type. The model card in the repository documents all of this.

KNOWN FAILURES

Where ShelfWatch gets it wrong

FailureCause
Flat bars, hanging itemsRare in training: missed, so space looks empty
Fridge door frameA plain strip passes the emptiness check
Fully empty shelf or shelf endShelves are found from their products
Long aisle at an angleFar products are tiny
False gaps overallAbout half of red gaps are real (0.54)

Hanging items: missed

Angled aisle: far end missed

Speaker notes: Known failures, honestly. In these test photos green is found, red is missed. Thin hanging items like toothbrushes are mostly missed, and so are products at the far end of an angled aisle. In real stores, flat chocolate bars are missed too. On fridges, the metal frame between two doors can look like a gap. Because shelves are found from the products standing on them, a completely empty shelf or an empty shelf end can be missed. And overall, about half of the red gaps are real, so a person still needs to check. Each has a clear fix, on the next slide.

VERSION 2

From “where is it empty?” to “what is missing, and act on it”

Find the shelves

Detect each shelf’s front edge (Hough lines), so empty shelves, shelf ends and door frames are handled.

Name the product

Read the price tag under each gap (OCR): “Gap · Lotus Biscoff · AED 9.00”. CLIP category as a fallback.

Learn from staff

One tap for “not a gap” or “missed this”, saved as training data: the model improves on local stores.

Later: shelf fullness over time and forecasting, a manager dashboard, and text-guided inpainting for realistic synthetic gaps.

Speaker notes: Version 2. First, find the shelves themselves using their straight front edges, which fixes empty shelves, shelf ends and fridge door frames. Second, name the missing product by reading the price tag under each gap with OCR, so the card says not just "gap" but "Lotus Biscoff, 9 dirhams". Third, let staff correct the app with one tap, and use those corrections to retrain on local stores, which targets the chocolate-bar problem directly. Later: fullness over time, forecasting and a manager dashboard.
